$comment: THE FLAG REGISTER (Task 043B, R4).
Every switch that decides what a user SEES or what the application DOES,
with the state it is in when nobody has decided otherwise, and the date by
which it must be deleted or re-justified.
WHY THIS IS A FILE AND NOT A PARAGRAPH
A flag list in a runbook drifts from the code on the day it is written, and
nothing notices. Here the gate reads the DECLARATION the deploy will
actually use - deploy/k8s/frontend/configmap.yaml, frontend/.env.example,
FeatureOptions.cs - and fails when the recorded default and the declared
default disagree. That disagreement is the whole failure: an operator
reading this file and a cluster running the other value.
R4: A FLAG IS CONFIGURATION, NEVER AUTHORIZATION
Two rules, and both are enforced rather than restated:
* every entry asserts `authorization: false`, and `gates` must be one of
presentation / behaviour / rollout / inert. The vocabulary has no word
for access on purpose, so a flag that starts gating a permission has
nowhere to declare it and the gate fails.
* no file under the authorization paths (src/DubbingPlatform.Api/Auth/
Security/, Policies/, Application/Authorization/,
Infrastructure/Identity/) may reference FeatureOptions, Features__ or
VITE_ENABLE_. That is the same property checked in the source rather
than in this file, because a register cannot see its own readers.
Access control keeps working when the flag is off, when the flag service is
unreachable, and when somebody flips it during an incident. Those three
conditions are the whole argument.
`reviewBy` IS NOT OPTIONAL (the task's edge case)
A flag nobody removes is a permanent, undocumented, untested code path
that only exists because it was cheap to add. Every entry carries a date,
and an entry past its date is a gate failure rather than a note - a flag
defaulted off that nobody has reviewed in two quarters may not be the right
shape any more, and nobody can find out while it is green.

flags.gatesWhat: the admin diagnostics surfaces. The endpoints stay reachable and stay authorized by the API; the flag decides whether the UI offers them.

product analytics collection. Off with no destination is the correct state: a flag whose collector does not exist is a flag nobody reads, and enabling it would only create a request that goes nowhere.

unfinished surfaces. The flag-off-means-absent contract is what makes a half-built surface safe to ship at all: the code is in the bundle, the surface is not reachable, and the flag is what makes it revertible without a redeploy.

error reporting. `sentry-disabled` is a non-empty, non-URL sentinel on purpose: an empty injected value passes an 'is it configured?' check and then initialises nothing, which is the failure mode the sentinel exists to make impossible.

flags.defaultScope: frontend/.env.example, which is the LOCAL DEVELOPMENT default. The deployed value is injected per environment by deploy/config-inject.sh, and this register records the committed default rather than each environment's.
flags.gatesWhat: live progress over SSE versus polling. Behaviour, not presentation: the workspace is usable either way, which is why the degraded path is a supported state rather than an error.
client telemetry emission. Never gates whether an event is AUTHORIZED to be recorded - that is the API's decision and its audit trail, and a browser-side switch cannot be the access control for it.

whether enrichment is REQUESTED. Dual-gated with the per-project setting; a project that does not ask for it never gets it regardless of this flag, which is why the flag is a rollout switch and not a permission.
whether lip-sync is REQUESTED. Same dual gate as above, and the same reason the flag is not authorization: a tenant that is not entitled to the capability cannot obtain it by the flag being on.

the local inference warm-up. It is a HEALTH check rather than a feature gate, which is why it is safe: when the flag is off the check reports Healthy and readiness is unaffected. A flag that gated readiness would gate traffic on configuration.
